subject: forensic-medicine
title: Trace Evidence: Semen Crystal Tests, Hair Microscopy and Locard Principle

steps.title: Microcrystalline semen assays: The Florence test
steps.tx: When microscopes fail to identify spermatozoa in aged stains, microcrystalline assays assist in detecting seminal chemical constituents. The historic **Florence test choline periodide assay** detects choline, a degradation product of lecithin secreted by the seminal vesicles. A drop of stain extract is treated with Florence reagent (potassium iodide and iodine in water). Under microscopy, dark brown, rhombic, needle-shaped, or lance-shaped crystals of choline periodide appear promptly.
steps.say: The Florence test mixes stain extract with iodine solution, precipitating dark brown needle-shaped crystals of choline periodide if semen is present.

nodes.label: Dried stain scrapings placed on glass slide
Addition of Florence reagent (iodine + potassium iodide in water)
Precipitation of brown rhombic choline periodide crystals

steps.tx: When spermatozoa are no longer visible in an aged stain, the **Florence test choline periodide assay** looks for choline, a breakdown product of lecithin secreted by the seminal vesicles. A drop of extract meets Florence reagent, potassium iodide and iodine in water. Microscopy promptly shows dark brown rhombic, needle shaped, or lance shaped crystals of choline periodide. The crystals support seminal origin but do not replace the finding of sperm when sperm are still present.
steps.say: Iodine reagent mixed with stain extract precipitates dark brown needles of choline periodide if seminal choline is present. The Florence crystals help when sperm heads can no longer be found.

vis.alt: Dark brown rhombic and needle shaped choline periodide crystals fill the microscopic field.
vis.caption: Florence reagent added to a stain extract throws down brown lance shaped crystals of choline periodide. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: The Barberio test for seminal spermine
steps.tx: Complementing choline testing, the **Barberio test spermine picrate assay** identifies spermine, a polyamine base secreted in high quantities by the human prostate gland. The unknown stain extract is treated with a saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid. Under microscopic examination, characteristic yellowish, slender, needle-shaped, rhomboid, or feather-like crystals of spermine picrate precipitate, providing supportive evidence of prostatic fluid.
steps.say: The Barberio test treats stain extract with picric acid, forming yellow feather-like crystals of spermine picrate from prostatic secretions.

steps.title: Forensic hair structure: Cuticle, cortex and medulla
steps.tx: Hair frequently transfers between victim and assailant during violent sexual assaults and struggles. In forensic trichology, the **trichological hair microscopic architecture** comprises three concentric cylindrical layers: the outer protective cuticle composed of overlapping keratinized scales, the intermediate cortex containing melanin pigment granules and cortical fusi that provide tensile strength, and the central core medulla containing cellular debris and air spaces.
steps.say: Hair consists of three layers: an outer scaled cuticle, a middle pigment-filled cortex, and a central core channel called the medulla.

rows: Distinguishes human hair from animal pelt scales
Dense spindle-shaped cells packed with melanin
Determines natural hair color, diameter, and mechanical strength
Central axial cellular channel or air column
Medullary index definitively separates human from animal hair
Provides nucleated cells for STR nuclear DNA profiling

steps.title: Human versus animal hair: The medullary index
steps.tx: The most definitive criterion distinguishing human from animal hair is the **medullary index mathematical ratio**, calculated by dividing the transverse diameter of the central medulla by the total diameter of the hair shaft. In human hair, the medulla is narrow, fragmented, or absent, yielding a medullary index of less than zero-point-three. In animal hair, the medulla is wide, continuous, and structured, producing an index exceeding zero-point-five.
steps.say: The medullary index separates human from animal hair: human hair has an index under 0.3, while animal hair has a wide medulla over 0.5.

left.title: Human hair
points: Medullary index: Under 0.3 (narrow medulla)
Medulla: Fragmented, interrupted, or absent
Cuticular scales: Imbricate, flattened, non-protruding
Pigment granules: Concentrated toward peripheral cortex

right.title: Animal hair
points: Medullary index: Over 0.5 (wide medulla)
Medulla: Broad, continuous, patterned (ladder/lattice)
Cuticular scales: Coronal, spinous, prominent petals
Pigment granules: Concentrated centrally around medulla

steps.tx: Human and animal hair are separated by the **medullary index mathematical ratio**, medulla width divided by total shaft width. Human medulla is narrow, fragmented, or absent, so the index stays below zero point three. Animal medulla is wide, continuous, and patterned, so the index exceeds zero point five. The broad lattice and the thin broken core in the comparison are therefore scored as that ratio.
steps.say: Divide medulla width by shaft width. Human hair scores under zero point three with a narrow or broken medulla, while animal hair scores over zero point five with a wide continuous medulla.

vis.alt: Human hair with a narrow broken medulla is compared with animal hair that has a wide continuous lattice medulla.
vis.caption: Side by side shafts show a thin fragmented human medulla against a broad continuous medulla filling much of an animal hair. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: Hair growth phases: Anagen, catagen and telogen
steps.tx: Forensic scientists examine the proximal root to determine the **follicular hair growth phase**, establishing whether hair was forcibly pulled or naturally shed. The anagen phase represents active mitotic growth (eighty-five percent of scalp hairs), possessing an elongated, nucleated follicular sheath rich in nuclear DNA. The catagen phase marks regression, while the telogen phase represents the resting club hair that sheds naturally without attached follicular tissue.
steps.say: Anagen hairs are actively growing and carry nucleated root sheaths for DNA testing, while telogen resting hairs shed naturally without DNA-rich roots.

nodes.label: Anagen phase (Active growth for 2 to 6 years, rich DNA sheath)
Catagen phase (Transitional involution spanning 2 to 3 weeks)
Telogen phase (Resting club hair lasting 3 to 4 months)

steps.title: Forensic differentiation between forcibly pulled and naturally shed hair
steps.tx: In physical assault cases, microscopists analyze the **forcibly extracted hair root morphology** to determine violence. Naturally shed hairs entering the telogen phase possess clean, dry, club-shaped bulbs devoid of attached cellular sheaths or blood. In contrast, hairs forcibly torn from a victim's scalp during physical violence display stretched, ruptured root sheaths, sheared cortical margins, irregular follicular tags, and adhering blood droplets.
steps.say: Naturally shed hairs have smooth, clean club roots. Forcibly pulled hairs have torn root sheaths, stretched bulbs, and attached blood droplets.

points: Smooth, dry, club-shaped root bulb

right.title: Forcibly extracted hair
points: Distorted, stretched, or fractured root bulb

Excellent source for nuclear STR profiling

steps.title: Forensic textile fiber classification
steps.tx: Transfer of clothing threads during struggles provides critical corroborative evidence via **forensic textile fiber analysis**. Fibers divide into natural fibers (vegetable cotton with twisted ribbon morphology, animal wool with surface scales, protein silk) and synthetic polymers (nylon, polyester, acrylic, polypropylene). Forensic examiners analyze fiber diameter, longitudinal striations, cross-sectional geometry, and dye spectrophotometry to match crime scene threads against suspect clothing.
steps.say: Clothing fibers transfer during struggles. Examiners analyze natural fibers like cotton and wool, and synthetic polymers like nylon, matching weave and color.

rows: Smooth, triangular cross-section with high sheen

steps.title: The Locard exchange principle in physical evidence
steps.tx: Underpinning all physical trace evidence recovery, the fundamental **Locard exchange principle axiom** formulated by French criminologist Edmond Locard holds that 'every contact leaves a trace'. Whenever two entities come into physical contact during a violent crime, there is a mutual, reciprocal transfer of physical material: the perpetrator leaves fibers, blood, or hairs at the scene, while carrying away carpet fibers, soil, or victim biology.
steps.say: Locard's exchange principle states that every contact leaves a trace: a criminal leaves evidence at the scene and takes trace materials away.

steps.title: Chain of custody and crime scene preservation
steps.tx: To ensure that recovered trace evidence withstands rigorous judicial scrutiny, maintaining an unbroken **trace evidence chain of custody** is legally mandatory. Forensic technicians must photograph trace items in situ, collect hairs and fibers using clean tweezers into separate paper envelopes, apply tamper-evident seals, and record every custodian who handles the evidence from the crime scene to the forensic science laboratory.
steps.say: Trace evidence must be photographed, collected with clean tweezers into sealed paper envelopes, and tracked through a strict chain of custody.
